highlightAliases.old: Evidence for prophylaxis in PJ (prosthetic joint) patients is even weaker than for prosthetic valves; despite this, the ADA recommends "considering" antibiotic prophylaxis for PJs at "high risk" — placed within 2 years, or in immunosuppressed patients (including diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, malnourishment), or with prior joint infection (p1674–1675)Current practice (not the book): in general, prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended before dental procedures to prevent prosthetic joint infection — ADA clinical practice guideline, 2015.
highlightAliases.new: Evidence for prophylaxis in PJ (prosthetic joint) patients is even weaker than for prosthetic valves; the historical discussion describes considering antibiotic prophylaxis for PJs deemed "high risk" — placed within 2 years, or in immunosuppressed patients (including diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, malnourishment), or with prior joint infection (p1674–1675)Current practice (not the book): in general, prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended before dental procedures to prevent prosthetic joint infection — ADA clinical practice guideline, 2015.

highlightAliases.old: Treatment is tiered: vancomycin first-line; fidaxomicin equivalent for cure and lowers relapse but costlier (limits first-line use); metronidazole no longer first-line "except in serious disease with vancomycin" (p1672); for C difficile colitis/toxic megacolon, vancomycin + metronidazole IV "if ileus or toxic megacolon" (p1673); vancomycin prophylaxis in patients with recent CDI needing further antibiotics reduces risk to 4% from 26% (p1672–1673, Table 104-1)
highlightAliases.new: For initial nonfulminant CDI, IDSA/SHEA favors fidaxomicin when feasible; oral vancomycin remains an acceptable alternative; metronidazole is not first-line monotherapy (p1672); for fulminant CDI, combine enteral vancomycin and IV metronidazole, especially with ileus (p1673); a study of patients with recent CDI needing other antibiotics reported recurrence of 4% with oral vancomycin prophylaxis versus 26% without it; this was a historical study result. AGA 2026 advises against giving vancomycin during systemic antibiotics for the purpose of CDI prevention (p1672–1673, Table 104-1; AGA, advice 12)

highlightAliases.old: Protein-energy malnutrition (PEM) affects 30–60% of hospitalized adults >65; even mild PEM (albumin 3.0–3.5 g/dL) blunts vaccine response (p1668)
highlightAliases.new: The chapter reports protein-energy malnutrition in 30–60% of hospitalized adults over 65 and reduced vaccine responses in outpatients with albumin 3.0–3.5 g/dL (p1668). Inflammation can lower albumin. Serum albumin alone cannot diagnose or grade malnutrition. ASPEN position paper

highlightAliases.old: Culture stewardship: almost universally, do NOT culture skin-surface swabs or urine in the presence of a long-term indwelling catheter — such cultures will always be positive but don't correlate with infection, are more often misleading than helpful, and should NOT guide antibiotic selection (KCP #3, p1668; reinforced p1671). Exception in Table 104-1: for catheter-associated urosepsis, "Culture to guide subsequent therapy" (p1673)
highlightAliases.new: Avoid routine surface swabs of pressure ulcers and surveillance urine cultures from asymptomatic catheterized residents. Colonization is common. For suspected symptomatic catheter-associated UTI, obtain a urine culture before antibiotics when feasible, including when sepsis is absent. Collect from the freshly placed catheter if it is replaced (pp1668, 1671, 1673; IDSA, recommendations 45–46).

highlightAliases.old: OPAT (outpatient parenteral antibiotic therapy) is covered by Medicare Part D at home but is underused; patients are often admitted to nursing homes instead just to obtain coverage (p1670)
highlightAliases.new: US home OPAT coverage depends on the drug, equipment, services and insurance benefit. Part D drug coverage alone does not establish coverage for supplies and nursing. Part B covers qualifying home infusion drugs, equipment and services. Coverage gaps can influence the discharge setting (p1670). Medicare, home infusion coverage

highlightAliases.old: Several small studies estimate 18F-FDG uptake in the temporal, maxillary, or vertebral arteries occurs in 64–82% of GCA patients, with very high specificity; some authors conclude temporal artery biopsy may be avoided when cranial-artery uptake is absent — corticosteroids for more than a few days can markedly reduce the sensitivity of both PET/CT and biopsy (p1676)
highlightAliases.new: Several small studies estimate 18F-FDG uptake in the temporal, maxillary, or vertebral arteries occurs in 64–82% of GCA patients, with very high specificity; those historical studies do not support ruling out GCA from a negative cranial PET alone. With persistent suspicion, investigate further. Do not delay treatment when clinical suspicion is strong, particularly with threatened vision (p1676; EULAR, principles A and C)

highlightAliases.old: Skin-surface swabs (eg, pressure ulcers) and urine cultures in the presence of a long-term indwelling catheter — such cultures will always be positive but do not correlate with infection; they are more often misleading than helpful and should NOT guide antibiotic selection (p1668, p1671).
highlightAliases.new: Routine superficial wound swabs and surveillance urine cultures in asymptomatic catheterized residents often detect colonization.

highlightAliases.old: Exception: in catheter-associated urosepsis, Table 104-1 says "Culture to guide subsequent therapy" (p1673).
highlightAliases.new: Compatible new symptoms justify a urine culture before treatment when feasible, even without sepsis. Culture the fresh catheter if replaced (pp1668, 1671, 1673).

highlightAliases.old: In what fraction of older adults with serious infection is fever absent, and what temperature defines fever in this population?
highlightAliases.new: In what fraction of older adults with serious infection is fever absent, and when can lower temperatures indicate fever in a nursing-home resident?

highlightAliases.old: Up to one-third; fever is still defined as ≥100.4°F/38°C, but lower baseline temperature and a blunted febrile response make many older adults never reach it (p1669).
highlightAliases.new: Up to one-third may have a serious infection without reaching the conventional 38°C threshold (p1669). For nursing-home residents, a single oral temperature above 37.8°C, repeated oral temperatures above 37.2°C, or a rise above usual temperature of more than 1.1°C can identify fever earlier. IDSA long-term-care fever guideline.

highlightAliases.old: Compare TST and IFGRA sensitivity for latent TB in older adults, and state which is now used for most latent TB testing and why.
highlightAliases.new: Which test for TB infection is preferred after BCG vaccination, and what is the limit of a positive result?

highlightAliases.old: TST ~70% vs IFGRA ~75% (IFGRA only minimally more sensitive); most latent TB testing is now done by IFGRA because it needs only a single blood draw (no return visit), doesn't need two-step testing in nursing home residents, and has greater interrater reliability and specificity (p1675).
highlightAliases.new: IGRA is preferred after BCG because the vaccine does not cause a positive blood test. It requires one blood draw. A positive IGRA or skin test warrants assessment for active TB before diagnosing latent infection (p1675).
